labeler_note: Stale reference. While both allow securitised assets, the 2025 text mandates strict compliance with the newly introduced Master Directions DOR.STR.REC.53/21.04, replacing the older generic conditions.

claim_a_snippet: Small Finance Banks are not distinctively categorized for priority sector targets and shall follow the standard scheduled commercial bank limits.
claim_b_snippet: Small Finance Banks have a mandated Total Priority Sector target of 75 per cent of ANBC or CEOBSE, whichever is higher.
section_b: Chapter II - Targets/Sub-targets for Priority sector
labeler_note: Regulatory scope conflict. The 2015 framework did not have a dedicated 75% PSL target bracket for Small Finance Banks, whereas the 2025 directive expressly isolates them with this much higher target.

claim_a_snippet: The limit for collateral-free agricultural loans is maintained at ₹ 1 lakh per borrower.
claim_b_snippet: The limit for collateral-free short-term agricultural loans, including loans for allied activities, has been raised from ₹ 1.60 lakh to ₹ 2.00 lakh per borrower.
labeler_note: Numerical mismatch in the cap for collateral-free agriculture loans, jumping from ₹1 lakh in 2015 to a revised limit of ₹2 lakh in 2025.

claim_a_snippet: Education loans to individuals for educational purposes including vocational courses up to ₹ 10 lakh irrespective of the sanctioned amount will be considered as eligible for priority sector.
claim_b_snippet: Loans to individuals for educational purposes including vocational courses up to ₹ 20 lakh irrespective of the sanctioned amount will be considered as eligible for priority sector.
labeler_note: Numerical mismatch in the cap for Education loans under PSL, increasing from ₹10 lakh in 2015 to ₹20 lakh in 2025.

claim_a_snippet: Advances extended in India against the incremental FCNR (B)/NRE deposits, qualifying for exemption from CRR/SLR requirements, as per the Reserve Bank’s circulars DBOD.No.Ret.BC.36/12.01.001/ 2013-14 dated August 14, 2013.
claim_b_snippet: The incremental advances extended out of the resources generated from the eligible incremental FCNR(B)/NRE deposits is calculated as the difference between outstanding advances in India as on March 7, 2014, and the current outstanding.
section_a: Chapter II - Computation of Adjusted Net Bank Credit
labeler_note: Calculation methodology conflict. The 2025 framework introduces a strict cutoff date (March 7, 2014) to calculate the difference for FCNR(B)/NRE deposit exemptions, replacing the broader 2015 reference.

claim_a_snippet: Banks should not deduct / net any amount like provisions, accrued interest, etc. from NBC.
claim_b_snippet: provisions, accrued interest, etc. from NBC. [Banks shall not deduct]
section_b: Chapter I - Computation of Adjusted Net Bank Credit
labeler_note: Both circulars explicitly prohibit banks from deducting provisions or accrued interest from the Net Bank Credit (NBC) when calculating priority sector targets.

claim_a_snippet: Investments by banks in securitised assets, representing loans to various categories of priority sector, except 'others' category, are eligible for classification under respective categories of priority sector depending on the underlying assets.
claim_b_snippet: Investments or any other items which are treated as eligible for classification under priority sector target/sub-target achievement, shall also form part of Adjusted Net Bank Credit.
section_a: Chapter IV - Investments by banks in securitised assets
section_b: Chapter II - Computation of Adjusted Net Bank Credit
labeler_note: Both frameworks agree that investments in eligible securitised assets can be classified under priority sector and included in the Adjusted Net Bank Credit.

claim_a_snippet: No loan related and adhoc service charges/inspection charges should be levied on priority sector loans up to ₹ 25,000.
claim_b_snippet: No loan related and adhoc service charges/inspection charges should be levied on priority sector loans up to ₹ 25,000.
section_a: Chapter V - Common guidelines - Service charges
section_b: Chapter X - Common guidelines - Service charges
labeler_note: Both documents maintain the exact same consumer protection rule preventing banks from levying service or inspection charges on small priority sector loans up to ₹ 25,000.

claim_a_snippet: Banks should provide acknowledgement for loan applications received under priority sector loans.
claim_b_snippet: Banks should provide acknowledgement for loan applications received under priority sector loans.
labeler_note: Both circulars mandate that banks must formally acknowledge the receipt of priority sector loan applications.

claim_a_snippet: A register/ electronic record should be maintained by the bank, wherein the date of receipt, sanction/rejection/disbursement with reasons thereof, etc., should be recorded. The register/electronic record should be made available to all inspecting agencies.
claim_b_snippet: A register/electronic record should be maintained by the bank, wherein the date of receipt, sanction/rejection/disbursement with reasons thereof, etc., should be recorded and made available to inspecting agencies.
section_a: Chapter V - Common guidelines - Application register
section_b: Chapter X - Common guidelines - Application register
labeler_note: Both documents require the maintenance of a rigorous physical or electronic register to track the lifecycle of priority sector loan applications for inspection purposes.

claim_a_snippet: The targets and sub-targets set under priority sector lending... are to be computed on the basis of the ANBC or Credit Equivalent Amount of Off-Balance Sheet Exposure, whichever is higher.
claim_b_snippet: The targets and sub-targets set under priority sector lending, to be computed on the basis of the ANBC/CEOBSE as applicable as on the corresponding date of the preceding year.
section_b: Chapter II - Targets/Sub-targets for Priority sector
labeler_note: Both regulations base the priority sector target calculations on whichever is higher between Adjusted Net Bank Credit (ANBC) or Credit Equivalent Amount of Off-Balance Sheet Exposure (CEOBSE).

claim_a_snippet: Banks should ensure that loans extended under priority sector are for approved purposes and the end use is continuously monitored.
claim_b_snippet: Banks should ensure that loans extended under priority sector are for approved purposes and the end use is continuously monitored.
section_a: Chapter V - Common guidelines - End-use monitoring
section_b: Chapter X - Common guidelines - End-use monitoring
labeler_note: Both circulars enforce the strict requirement that banks must actively monitor the end-use of funds disbursed under priority sector lending.

claim_a_snippet: Housing loans to banks’ own employees will not be eligible for classification under the priority sector.
claim_b_snippet: Housing loans to banks’ own employees will not be eligible for classification under the priority sector.
labeler_note: Both documents explicitly exclude housing loans granted to a bank's own staff from being counted towards priority sector lending targets.

claim_a_snippet: Housing loans which are backed by long term bonds shall not be classified under priority sector, as they are exempted from inclusion in ANBC.
claim_b_snippet: Housing loans which are backed by long term bonds shall not be classified under priority sector, as they are exempted from inclusion in ANBC.
section_a: Chapter III - Housing - Long-term bond backed loans
section_b: Chapter II - Housing - Long-term bond backed loans
labeler_note: Both texts agree that housing loans funded by long-term bonds are carved out of ANBC and thus cannot be double-counted as priority sector achievements.

claim_a_snippet: Non-achievement of priority sector targets and sub-targets will be taken into account while granting regulatory clearances/approvals for various purposes.
claim_b_snippet: Non-achievement of priority sector targets and sub-targets will be taken into account while granting regulatory clearances/approvals for various purposes.
section_b: Chapter VIII - Non-achievement of priority sector targets
labeler_note: Both circulars threaten regulatory penalties, noting that failure to meet PSL targets will negatively impact a bank's ability to secure RBI regulatory clearances and approvals.

claim_a_snippet: A Large Corporate (LC) is defined as a listed entity with outstanding long-term borrowings of Rs 100 crore or above.
claim_b_snippet: A Core Investment Company (CIC) is subject to Scale Based Regulation if its asset size is Rs 100 crore and above, irrespective of borrowing levels.
labeler_note: Numerical and scope mismatch for regulatory trigger. SEBI relies on borrowing threshold (Rs 100 cr), while RBI relies on asset size threshold (Rs 100 cr).

claim_a_snippet: LCs shall mandate raising a minimum of 25% of their incremental borrowings during the financial year through the issuance of debt securities.
claim_b_snippet: CICs shall ensure that outside liabilities do not exceed 2.5 times of their Adjusted Net Worth and are heavily restricted from issuing public debt.
labeler_note: Direct policy conflict for a CIC that qualifies as an LC. SEBI mandates 25% market borrowing, whereas RBI restricts CICs from certain public debt issuances and limits leverage.

claim_a_snippet: The framework applies to all listed entities excluding Scheduled Commercial Banks.
claim_b_snippet: The Scale Based Regulation framework applies to all NBFCs including CICs, categorized into Base, Middle, Upper, and Top Layers.
labeler_note: Scope conflict. SEBI excludes SCBs but includes NBFCs/CICs automatically if listed, while RBI applies layered regulations regardless of listing status.

claim_a_snippet: Outstanding long-term borrowings shall mean any outstanding borrowing with an original maturity of more than 1 year.
claim_b_snippet: Outside liabilities mean all forms of borrowings, including short-term and long-term debt, regardless of maturity.
labeler_note: Definitional mismatch on what constitutes borrowing/liabilities. SEBI excludes short-term debt (<1 year) for the LC threshold, while RBI includes all outside liabilities.

claim_a_snippet: Details of incremental borrowings shall be disclosed to the stock exchanges within 45 days of the end of the financial year.
claim_b_snippet: CICs must submit their annual financial returns and leverage details to the Reserve Bank within 15 days from the date of finalization of the balance sheet.
labeler_note: Reporting timeline conflict. SEBI requires exchange disclosure within 45 days of FY end, whereas RBI mandates submission within 15 days of balance sheet finalization.

claim_a_snippet: In case of a shortfall in the requisite borrowing through debt securities, a penalty of 0.2% of the shortfall shall be levied.
claim_b_snippet: Regulatory penalties for non-compliance with leverage and investment norms for CICs shall be determined purely by the RBI Adjudication Committee without a fixed percentage.
labeler_note: Penalty structure mismatch. SEBI prescribes a fixed 0.2% financial penalty for borrowing shortfalls, while RBI utilizes discretionary supervisory penalties.

claim_a_snippet: The framework is applicable to entities having a credit rating of AA and above.
claim_b_snippet: The SBR framework categorization does not depend on credit ratings, but purely on asset size, group structure, and systemic importance.
section_b: Chapter 1 - Base Layer and Middle Layer Criteria
labeler_note: Trigger mismatch. SEBI uses AA credit rating as a strict gate for LC classification, whereas RBI explicitly ignores credit ratings for SBR layer placement.

claim_a_snippet: The compliance regarding the 25% borrowing requirement shall be tested over a contiguous block of three years.
claim_b_snippet: Compliance with Adjusted Net Worth and Leverage requirements must be maintained continuously and reported on an annual basis.
labeler_note: Measurement frequency mismatch. SEBI allows a 3-year block to smooth out borrowing compliance, whereas RBI requires continuous and strict annual compliance.

claim_a_snippet: 'Incremental borrowings' shall exclude any borrowings from parent entities or related parties.
claim_b_snippet: 'Outside liabilities' strictly include borrowings from group companies, parent entities, and related party debt.
labeler_note: Direct conflict in liability calculation. SEBI excludes related-party debt from LC borrowing obligations, while RBI specifically includes it in CIC leverage ratios.

claim_a_snippet: The mandatory borrowing requirement applies to incremental borrowings raised during the FY exceeding Rs 50 crore.
claim_b_snippet: All borrowings, regardless of the incremental amount raised during the FY, are subject to the 2.5x leverage ceiling.
labeler_note: Threshold mismatch. SEBI ignores incremental borrowing under Rs 50 cr, whereas RBI caps all borrowings regardless of the incremental quantum.

claim_a_snippet: Disclosure must be certified jointly by the Company Secretary and the Chief Financial Officer (CFO).
claim_b_snippet: Regulatory returns to the RBI must be signed exclusively by the Managing Director or the Chief Executive Officer.
labeler_note: Signatory mismatch for compliance reporting. SEBI requires CS and CFO joint certification, whereas RBI strictly requires MD/CEO signature.

claim_a_snippet: Funds raised through debt securities under this framework can be deployed for any general corporate purpose including onward lending.
claim_b_snippet: CICs are strictly prohibited from engaging in any other financial activity other than investment in group companies and cannot do general onward lending.
section_a: Chapter III - End Use of Funds
labeler_note: End-use conflict. SEBI permits funds raised to be used for general lending, while RBI restricts CICs entirely to group company investments.

claim_a_snippet: Listed entities shall use the standard definition of 'Net Worth' as per Section 2(57) of the Companies Act, 2013.
claim_b_snippet: CICs shall use 'Adjusted Net Worth' (ANW) which includes unrealized appreciation in book value of investments up to 50%.
labeler_note: Accounting conflict. SEBI relies on the standard Companies Act Net Worth, whereas RBI dictates a specialized 'Adjusted Net Worth' formula for CICs.

claim_a_snippet: The stock exchanges shall collect the penalty amount directly from the listed entity for the Investor Protection Fund.
claim_b_snippet: Any penalty levied on the NBFC-CIC shall be deposited directly into the designated Reserve Bank of India penalty account.
labeler_note: Jurisdictional conflict over penalty collection. SEBI routes fines to the exchange's IPF, while RBI routes fines to its own designated accounts.

claim_a_snippet: The framework shall not apply to entities that are in the process of resolving stressed assets under the IBC.
claim_b_snippet: CICs undergoing restructuring or IBC proceedings remain fully subject to SBR reporting and compliance unless specifically exempted by RBI.
labeler_note: Applicability conflict during distress. SEBI automatically exempts IBC companies, while RBI maintains standard regulatory applicability.

claim_a_snippet: Entities must obtain a fresh credit rating for any incremental debt securities issued under this mandate.
claim_b_snippet: CICs are not mandated to obtain external credit ratings for their standard inter-group liabilities.
labeler_note: Operational mismatch. SEBI requires fresh ratings for LC debt issuances, while RBI does not require external ratings for CIC group funding.

claim_a_snippet: The framework considers Non-Convertible Debentures (NCDs) as the primary instrument for fulfilling the 25% mandate.
claim_b_snippet: Issuance of NCDs by CICs requires explicit prior approval from the RBI if it exceeds 10% of their Net Owned Fund.
labeler_note: Instrument viability conflict. SEBI pushes NCDs as the primary compliance tool, while RBI heavily restricts and requires prior approval for CIC NCD issuances.

claim_a_snippet: Reporting of borrowing blocks shall align with the standard Financial Year (April 1 to March 31).
claim_b_snippet: For certain regulatory ratios, CICs may be required to align reporting based on the calendar year if foreign parents are involved.
labeler_note: Timeline discrepancy. SEBI strictly enforces the April-March FY, while RBI SBR allows calendar year reporting flexibility for foreign-owned entities.

claim_a_snippet: In case of mergers, the borrowing requirement of the resultant entity will be recalculated from the date of the merger.
claim_b_snippet: In case of restructuring or mergers involving a CIC, the historical leverage limits and layer classification remain intact for the financial year.
labeler_note: Treatment of corporate actions mismatch. SEBI resets the borrowing block on merger, while RBI carries over the historical classification and limits.

claim_a_snippet: External Commercial Borrowings (ECBs) are explicitly excluded from the calculation of incremental borrowings.
claim_b_snippet: ECBs are strictly included in the calculation of Outside Liabilities for the purpose of the 2.5x leverage ratio.
labeler_note: Calculation conflict regarding ECBs. SEBI excludes them from the LC threshold/mandate, while RBI counts them fully against the CIC leverage cap.

claim_a_snippet: A 'Group' shall be determined as per the definitions laid out in the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015.
claim_b_snippet: 'Group companies' shall mean an arrangement involving two or more entities related to each other through the definition provided in the RBI Act, 1934.
labeler_note: Definitional conflict. SEBI utilizes LODR definitions for group entities, whereas RBI strictly uses the statutory RBI Act definition.

claim_a_snippet: Board size for Large Corporates must have a minimum of 6 directors to ensure proper governance over debt raising.
claim_b_snippet: CICs in the Middle and Upper layers must have a minimum of 3 directors on their Board.
labeler_note: Governance mismatch. SEBI requires at least 6 directors for LCs, whereas RBI SBR requires only a minimum of 3 directors.

claim_a_snippet: The Risk Management Committee must meet at least twice a year to review borrowing compliance.
claim_b_snippet: The Risk Management Committee of NBFCs in the Upper Layer must meet at least quarterly.
labeler_note: Meeting frequency mismatch. SEBI sets a biannual baseline for RMC meetings, while RBI mandates quarterly meetings for higher-layer NBFCs.

claim_a_snippet: A Large Corporate cannot place debt securities privately with its own promoter group to fulfill the 25% criteria.
claim_b_snippet: CICs are encouraged to raise funds through private placement primarily from group companies and promoters to limit public risk.
labeler_note: Funding source conflict. SEBI explicitly bans using promoter debt to meet the LC mandate, while RBI prefers CICs to fund exclusively via promoters/group.

claim_a_snippet: Statutory Auditors must certify the initial disclosure regarding LC status within 30 days of the FY start.
claim_b_snippet: Statutory Auditors must submit their certificate regarding the CIC's compliance with asset and income patterns within 60 days of the FY end.
labeler_note: Audit timeline mismatch. SEBI requires an upfront auditor certification (30 days from FY start), while RBI requires an end-of-year certification (60 days from FY end).

claim_a_snippet: Any relaxation from the borrowing framework requirements must be sought from the SEBI Corporation Finance Department.
claim_b_snippet: Any exemptions from Scale Based Regulation norms must be approved by the Department of Regulation, RBI.
labeler_note: Jurisdictional conflict for relief. A dual-regulated CIC/LC must apply to entirely different regulatory bodies for operational exemptions.

claim_a_snippet: A maximum of 5% of the total borrowing can be raised via short-term commercial paper if the LC mandate is met.
claim_b_snippet: CICs are permitted to issue Commercial Paper up to 100% of their net worth subject to RBI guidelines.
labeler_note: Instrument cap mismatch. SEBI caps CP usage relative to total borrowing for LCs, whereas RBI permits CICs high flexibility with CP based on net worth.

claim_a_snippet: Listed entities must maintain a public website displaying their LC status and borrowing block calculations.
claim_b_snippet: Unlisted CICs, even if part of a listed group, are not required to maintain a public website for regulatory disclosures.
labeler_note: Disclosure medium conflict. SEBI mandates public website disclosure for LC metrics, while RBI does not require a public website for standard CIC reporting.

claim_a_snippet: The framework mandates that at least 50% of the independent directors must approve the annual LC borrowing plan.
claim_b_snippet: All funding plans and leverage strategies of a CIC must be approved by a unanimous vote of the Board of Directors.
labeler_note: Voting threshold mismatch. SEBI requires a 50% ID majority for borrowing plans, while RBI strictly requires unanimous Board approval.

claim_a_snippet: In the event of default on debt securities, the LC classification is temporarily suspended for a period of one year.
claim_b_snippet: In the event of default on any liability, a CIC is immediately reclassified into the Top Layer for enhanced supervisory intervention.
labeler_note: Consequence of default mismatch. SEBI suspends the LC mandate during default, whereas RBI aggressively elevates the regulatory burden by moving the entity to the Top Layer.

claim_a_snippet: The Board of Directors must formulate a comprehensive policy regarding the borrowing strategy and risk management.
claim_b_snippet: The Board of Directors of the NBFC shall frame a Board approved policy for resource planning and risk mitigation.
labeler_note: Both frameworks align on the core requirement that the Board of Directors must establish policies for borrowing/resource planning and risk management.

claim_a_snippet: Entities must appoint a designated Compliance Officer responsible for ensuring adherence to the borrowing requirements.
claim_b_snippet: Every NBFC must designate a senior management executive as the Chief Compliance Officer to oversee regulatory adherence.
labeler_note: Both regulators strictly require the appointment of a dedicated Compliance Officer/CCO to monitor regulatory adherence.

claim_a_snippet: The entity shall not use the proceeds of the borrowing for any activities strictly prohibited by law or for speculative equity trading.
claim_b_snippet: CICs shall not deploy their funds in speculative activities, trading in real estate, or any prohibited non-financial activities.
labeler_note: Both frameworks expressly prohibit the deployment of raised funds/resources into speculative or legally prohibited activities.

claim_a_snippet: All records pertaining to the issuance of debt securities and board resolutions must be preserved for a minimum of eight years.
claim_b_snippet: NBFCs shall preserve records of all board approvals, liabilities, and statutory filings for a period not less than eight years.
labeler_note: Both SEBI and RBI align on the standard 8-year record preservation requirement for board decisions and financial filings.

claim_a_snippet: Any change in the Chief Financial Officer must be reported to the stock exchanges within 24 hours.
claim_b_snippet: Changes in Key Managerial Personnel (including the CFO) must be intimated to the Reserve Bank within the stipulated timeline.
labeler_note: Both regulatory bodies require mandatory and timely reporting when there is a change in Key Managerial Personnel like the CFO.

claim_a_snippet: The Statutory Auditor of the entity shall be subject to rotation as per the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013.
claim_b_snippet: NBFCs shall enforce the rotation of statutory auditors in strict alignment with the timelines prescribed under the Companies Act, 2013.
labeler_note: Both frameworks defer to and enforce the auditor rotation rules exactly as defined in the Companies Act, 2013.

claim_a_snippet: Entities must maintain adequate internal controls and systems to monitor the utilization of borrowed funds.
claim_b_snippet: The Board shall ensure that a robust Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Process and internal control system is in place.
labeler_note: Both documents mandate the establishment of robust internal controls and systems to monitor resources and compliance.

claim_a_snippet: Material events, including defaults or credit rating downgrades, must be disclosed immediately to avoid market asymmetry.
claim_b_snippet: Any material adverse event, such as a downgrade in credit rating or default, must be reported to the regulator without delay.
labeler_note: Both SEBI and RBI emphasize the immediate reporting/disclosure of material adverse events like defaults or rating downgrades.

claim_a_snippet: The framework promotes transparency and accountability in the debt markets and corporate balance sheets.
claim_b_snippet: The Scale Based Regulation is designed to enhance transparency, governance, and systemic stability in the NBFC sector.
labeler_note: Both documents share a unified overarching objective of promoting transparency, accountability, and stability in corporate operations.

claim_a_snippet: Non-compliance with these guidelines may result in regulatory action, financial penalties, or restrictions on future market access.
claim_b_snippet: Failure to comply with the SBR directives will attract penal action under the RBI Act, which may include restrictions on business operations.
labeler_note: Both frameworks establish clear consequences for non-compliance, including penalties and restrictions on future operations.

claim_a_snippet: Continual disclosures of trades by promoters, designated persons, and directors must be made to the company within 2 trading days if the traded value exceeds Rs. 10 Lakhs.
claim_b_snippet: Any changes in beneficial ownership by directors or officers are not reported on Form 8-K, but must be filed separately under Section 16 using Form 4 within 2 business days.
section_a: Chapter III - Disclosures of Trading by Insiders
section_b: General Instructions - Information to be Included
labeler_note: Scope and mechanism mismatch. SEBI integrates insider trade reporting into the primary PIT framework, whereas the SEC excludes standard insider trades from Form 8-K entirely, reserving them for Form 4.

claim_a_snippet: The company shall notify the particulars of such trading to the stock exchange on which the securities are listed within two trading days of receipt of the disclosure.
claim_b_snippet: A Current Report on Form 8-K shall be filed or furnished within four business days after the occurrence of the event specified in the items of this form.
section_b: General Instructions - B. Events to be Reported
labeler_note: Numerical discrepancy in public reporting deadlines. SEBI mandates stock exchange notification within 2 trading days, whereas SEC allows 4 business days for material event filing.

claim_a_snippet: Unpublished Price Sensitive Information (UPSI) shall be handled on a 'need to know' basis and shall not be communicated except for legitimate purposes.
claim_b_snippet: Under Regulation FD, whenever an issuer discloses material nonpublic information to certain enumerated persons, it must make public disclosure of that information promptly via Item 7.01 of Form 8-K.
labeler_note: Procedural conflict. SEBI permits sharing UPSI internally if recorded for 'legitimate purposes' without immediate public disclosure, whereas SEC Reg FD forces immediate public Form 8-K disclosure if shared with enumerated external parties.

claim_a_snippet: The board of directors shall ensure that a structured digital database is maintained containing the names of such persons with whom UPSI is shared and the nature of the UPSI.
claim_b_snippet: Issuers must maintain disclosure controls and procedures to capture material events for Form 8-K, but there is no specific statutory requirement to maintain a time-stamped digital database of all individuals who receive material nonpublic information.
labeler_note: Scope mismatch on internal tracking. SEBI mandates a strict, time-stamped 'Structured Digital Database' (SDD) for tracking UPSI sharing. SEC has no direct SDD equivalent under Form 8-K rules.

claim_a_snippet: Trading restriction period shall be made applicable from the end of every quarter till 48 hours after the declaration of financial results.
claim_b_snippet: Form 8-K Item 2.02 requires the furnishing of public announcements regarding results of operations, but Form 8-K does not govern or mandate specific insider trading window closures.
section_a: Schedule B - Minimum Standards for Trading
labeler_note: Regulatory scope mismatch. SEBI uses the PIT regulations to strictly mandate when trading windows must close globally for the company. SEC 8-K only mandates the filing of the financials, leaving blackout periods to internal corporate policy.

claim_a_snippet: Information filed with the stock exchanges under these regulations is deemed to be generally available information.
claim_b_snippet: Information furnished under Item 2.02 or Item 7.01 of Form 8-K is not deemed 'filed' for purposes of Section 18 of the Exchange Act and is not subject to the liabilities of that section.
labeler_note: Legal liability mismatch. SEBI treats all exchange submissions equally as generally available. SEC strictly distinguishes between 'furnished' (no Section 18 liability) and 'filed' information.

claim_a_snippet: A trading plan once approved shall be irrevocable and the insider shall mandatorily have to implement the plan, without being entitled to either deviate from it or execute any trade outside its scope.
claim_b_snippet: While officers may utilize 10b5-1 plans, Form 8-K does not govern the irrevocability of trading plans, and US case law generally permits the good-faith cancellation of a 10b5-1 plan.
labeler_note: Scope and policy conflict. SEBI strictly forbids the cancellation of an approved trading plan. Form 8-K (and broader SEC framework) does not mandate absolute irrevocability of trading plans.

claim_a_snippet: An informant who submits a Voluntary Information Disclosure Form may be eligible for a reward up to Rupees Ten Crores.
claim_b_snippet: The Form 8-K framework contains no provisions for whistleblower or informant rewards regarding the failure to file material events.
labeler_note: Numerical and scope mismatch. SEBI integrates a specific Rs 10 Crore informant reward mechanism directly into the PIT framework. SEC handles whistleblower rewards entirely outside the Form 8-K rulebook.

claim_a_snippet: A Compliance Officer shall be designated and shall be responsible for compliance of policies, procedures, maintenance of records, and monitoring adherence to the rules for the preservation of UPSI.
claim_b_snippet: The Form 8-K must be signed by an officer duly authorized by the registrant, typically the Chief Executive Officer or Chief Financial Officer, without mandating a separate statutory 'Compliance Officer' role.
labeler_note: Governance mismatch. SEBI requires a dedicated, designated 'Compliance Officer' to administer insider trading codes. SEC 8-K simply requires an 'authorized officer' to sign the filing.

claim_a_snippet: Any contra trade executed by a designated person within a period of six months from the prior transaction shall be rolled back and profits disgorged to the Board (SEBI).
claim_b_snippet: The Form 8-K rules do not contain short-swing profit rules. Disgorgement for trades within six months is governed strictly by Section 16(b), not the Current Report framework.
labeler_note: Scope mismatch. SEBI includes the 6-month contra-trade prohibition directly within the Insider Trading regulations. SEC enforces this via Section 16(b), entirely separate from Form 8-K.

claim_a_snippet: Any amount collected by the company for violations of the code of conduct shall be remitted to the Board for credit to the Investor Protection and Education Fund (IPEF).
claim_b_snippet: The SEC does not direct penalties for late 8-K filings into an Investor Protection Fund administered by the registrant; penalties are levied directly by the SEC to the US Treasury or Fair Fund.
labeler_note: Penalty routing mismatch. SEBI requires the company itself to collect fines from its employees for code violations and remit them to SEBI's IPEF. SEC 8-K violations are penalized directly by the regulator.

claim_a_snippet: Material events such as changes in key managerial personnel must be disclosed promptly as they constitute UPSI.
claim_b_snippet: Item 5.02 requires filing an 8-K within 4 business days if a principal executive officer, president, principal financial officer, or principal accounting officer retires, resigns, or is terminated.
section_b: Item 5.02 - Departure of Directors or Officers
labeler_note: Timeline discrepancy for personnel changes. SEBI requires prompt disclosure to cure UPSI status, while SEC explicitly grants a 4-business-day window for C-suite departures.

claim_a_snippet: The resignation of a statutory auditor does not have a specific disclosure annexure under PIT, but falls under general material information.
claim_b_snippet: Item 4.01 mandates a Form 8-K filing upon the resignation or dismissal of the independent accountant, explicitly requiring disclosure of any disagreements over accounting principles or practices in the prior two years.
section_b: Item 4.01 - Changes in Registrant's Certifying Accountant
labeler_note: Reporting depth mismatch. SEC 8-K requires highly specific, granular disclosures regarding disagreements with departing auditors. SEBI PIT broadly captures auditor changes as UPSI without the detailed disagreement framework.

claim_a_snippet: No safe harbor from regulatory action is provided for failing to disclose UPSI or failing to close the trading window.
claim_b_snippet: Failure to file an 8-K for certain items (e.g., 1.01, 1.02, 2.03) shall not be deemed a violation of Section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5, providing a limited safe harbor from anti-fraud liability.
labeler_note: Liability framework conflict. SEC provides an explicit safe harbor from 10b-5 (anti-fraud/insider trading) liability for failing to file certain 8-K items. SEBI offers no such safe harbor for failing to disclose UPSI.

claim_a_snippet: A major expansion of business or execution of new projects is deemed UPSI regardless of a fixed percentage of total assets.
claim_b_snippet: Item 2.01 requires an 8-K filing for the acquisition or disposition of a significant amount of assets, defined specifically as exceeding 10% of the registrant's total assets.
section_b: Item 2.01 - Completion of Acquisition or Disposition
labeler_note: Threshold discrepancy. SEC sets a hard 10% asset threshold to trigger an 8-K for asset sales. SEBI PIT treats major asset/project changes as UPSI qualitatively without a hard 10% statutory floor.

claim_a_snippet: Connected persons include any person who has been associated with the company in any capacity during the six months prior to the concerned act.
claim_b_snippet: Form 8-K obligations regarding related parties and directors are based on current status and Item 404 of Regulation S-K, without a blanket 'six-month lookback' for connected status.
labeler_note: Definitional mismatch. SEBI applies a broad 6-month retrospective lookback to classify someone as a 'connected person'. SEC 8-K relies on current executive/director status or specific related-party transaction thresholds.

claim_a_snippet: Off-market inter-se transfers between insiders who are in possession of the same UPSI are permitted as a valid defense against insider trading charges.
claim_b_snippet: Form 8-K provides no defense or exemptions for off-market inter-se transfers between insiders regarding material nonpublic information.
labeler_note: Defense mechanism conflict. SEBI explicitly carves out an exception for insiders trading with each other off-market while holding the same UPSI. SEC/8-K framework does not offer this specific defense.

claim_a_snippet: Firms must formulate a Code of Fair Disclosure and Conduct to regulate, monitor, and report trading by its designated persons.
claim_b_snippet: Item 5.05 requires an 8-K filing if the registrant amends its code of ethics that applies to its principal executive officer, principal financial officer, or principal accounting officer.
section_a: Chapter IV - Codes of Fair Disclosure
section_b: Item 5.05 - Amendments to the Registrant's Code of Ethics
labeler_note: Scope mismatch. SEBI regulates the creation and enforcement of the trading code itself. SEC 8-K strictly regulates the public disclosure of any amendments or waivers to the pre-existing code of ethics.

claim_a_snippet: If a director resigns, it is material information and must be reported to the exchange as UPSI.
claim_b_snippet: Under Item 5.02(a), if a director resigns due to a disagreement with the registrant on any matter relating to operations, policies, or practices, a detailed summary of the disagreement must be filed.
section_b: Item 5.02(a) - Resignation of Director due to Disagreement
labeler_note: Reporting depth mismatch. SEBI treats director resignation as standard UPSI. SEC 8-K explicitly forces the public disclosure of the internal disagreement that caused the resignation, going much deeper into corporate governance.

claim_a_snippet: Financial results must be submitted promptly, and the trading window must remain closed until 48 hours after they become generally available.
claim_b_snippet: Item 2.02 requires furnishing financial results to the SEC within 4 business days of any public announcement or release disclosing material non-public financial information.
section_b: Item 2.02 - Results of Operations and Financial Condition
labeler_note: Timeline discrepancy. SEBI links financial results to a strict 48-hour post-release trading window ban. SEC 8-K focuses merely on furnishing the release within 4 business days of its public announcement.

claim_a_snippet: Discovery of materially false financial statements triggers immediate UPSI disclosure obligations to prevent insider trading.
claim_b_snippet: Item 4.02 requires an 8-K filing if the board concludes that any previously issued financial statements can no longer be relied upon due to an error.
section_b: Item 4.02 - Non-Reliance on Previously Issued Financial Statements
labeler_note: Procedural mechanism mismatch. SEBI broadly treats false financials as UPSI requiring prompt disclosure. SEC has a highly specific 'Non-Reliance' trigger (Item 4.02) dictating exact steps when past financials are invalidated.

claim_a_snippet: The board of directors shall specify designated persons to be covered by the code of conduct based on their role and function.
claim_b_snippet: Form 8-K Item 5.02 specifically targets Named Executive Officers (NEOs) and directors, rather than requiring the board to define a custom list of 'designated persons'.
section_b: Item 5.02 - Compensatory Arrangements of Certain Officers
labeler_note: Target audience mismatch. SEBI requires the board to actively identify and list 'designated persons'. SEC 8-K relies on statutory definitions of NEOs and directors for its disclosure triggers.

claim_a_snippet: A trading plan shall entail commencement of trading on behalf of the insider no earlier than six months from the public disclosure of the plan.
claim_b_snippet: Form 8-K does not mandate a six-month cooling-off period for trading plans. (Note: SEC Rule 10b5-1 dictates cooling-off periods, but Form 8-K itself does not regulate this).
labeler_note: Scope mismatch. SEBI builds strict trading plan cooling-off periods directly into the core PIT rules. Form 8-K does not address trading plan mechanics.

claim_a_snippet: Creation of a pledge on securities by a designated person is considered trading and requires prior disclosure and pre-clearance.
claim_b_snippet: Form 8-K does not require reporting when an officer pledges company stock; such actions are typically reported via Section 16 Form 4 filings.
labeler_note: Reporting vehicle mismatch. SEBI defines pledging as 'trading' requiring immediate PIT compliance/disclosure. SEC 8-K ignores pledging, leaving it to Form 4 filings.

claim_a_snippet: Information regarding the delisting of securities is explicitly classified as Unpublished Price Sensitive Information.
claim_b_snippet: Item 3.01 requires filing an 8-K upon receiving a notice from a national securities exchange that the registrant does not satisfy a rule or standard for continued listing.
section_b: Item 3.01 - Notice of Delisting or Failure to Satisfy Listing Rule
labeler_note: Trigger threshold mismatch. SEBI broadly classifies 'delisting' as UPSI. SEC 8-K precisely triggers upon the receipt of a deficiency notice from the exchange, not just the delisting event itself.

claim_a_snippet: The regulations restrict trading when in possession of UPSI regarding a scheme of arrangement or merger.
claim_b_snippet: Item 1.01 requires an 8-K filing when the registrant enters into a material definitive agreement not made in the ordinary course of business, such as a merger agreement.
section_b: Item 1.01 - Entry into a Material Definitive Agreement
labeler_note: Conceptual focus mismatch. SEBI focuses on prohibiting trading before the merger is public. SEC 8-K focuses on forcing the disclosure of the definitive merger agreement once signed.

claim_a_snippet: Reporting obligations for designated persons apply universally on all trading days, regardless of weekends.
claim_b_snippet: For Form 8-K filings, if the due date falls on a Saturday, Sunday, or federal holiday, the filing is due on the next business day.
labeler_note: Deadline calculation mismatch. SEBI calculates based on 'trading days'. SEC calculates based on 'business days' and explicitly rolls over weekend deadlines.

claim_a_snippet: Any trades executed without pre-clearance by a designated person will result in disciplinary action under the code of conduct.
claim_b_snippet: Form 8-K does not require or regulate the pre-clearance of trades for company officers or directors.
labeler_note: Operational compliance mismatch. SEBI mandates an internal pre-clearance mechanism for insiders. SEC 8-K contains no pre-clearance mandates.

claim_a_snippet: Changes in capital structure are defined as Unpublished Price Sensitive Information requiring careful handling.
claim_b_snippet: Item 3.02 requires an 8-K filing for the unregistered sale of equity securities if they constitute 1% or more of the outstanding shares of that class.
section_b: Item 3.02 - Unregistered Sales of Equity Securities
labeler_note: Threshold discrepancy. SEBI broadly tags capital structure changes as UPSI. SEC 8-K requires an explicit filing specifically for unregistered equity sales hitting a 1% volume threshold.

claim_a_snippet: There are no specific provisions regarding the status of Shell Companies in the context of disclosing UPSI.
claim_b_snippet: Item 5.06 requires a Form 8-K filing when a registrant ceases to be a shell company, detailing the material terms of the transaction.
section_b: Item 5.06 - Change in Shell Company Status
labeler_note: Scope mismatch. SEC 8-K has a dedicated filing trigger for changes in Shell Company status. SEBI PIT does not isolate shell company status changes as a distinct reporting category.

claim_a_snippet: The objective is to prohibit insider trading and protect the integrity of the securities market by preventing information asymmetry.
claim_b_snippet: The Form 8-K requirements are designed to provide investors with timely disclosure of material corporate events to maintain fair and efficient markets.
labeler_note: Both frameworks share the exact same fundamental objective: ensuring market integrity by preventing information asymmetry and mandating timely disclosure of material events.

claim_a_snippet: Information that is likely to materially affect the price of the securities must be disclosed.
claim_b_snippet: Registrants must file Form 8-K to report the occurrence of events that are material to investors and the market.
section_b: General Instructions - Events to be Reported
labeler_note: Both frameworks revolve entirely around the concept of 'materiality'—requiring the disclosure of information that would influence an investor's decision.

claim_a_snippet: No insider shall communicate, provide, or allow access to any UPSI to any person except where such communication is in furtherance of legitimate purposes.
claim_b_snippet: Regulation FD prohibits the selective disclosure of material nonpublic information to market professionals or shareholders unless it is simultaneously disclosed to the public.
labeler_note: Both regulatory sets strictly prohibit the selective disclosure of material, non-public information to favored individuals.

claim_a_snippet: The compliance officer and the board of directors are responsible for administering the code of conduct and ensuring disclosures are made.
claim_b_snippet: The Form 8-K must be signed by an officer duly authorized by the registrant, placing accountability for the disclosure on senior corporate officers.
section_a: Chapter IV - Codes of Fair Disclosure
labeler_note: Both frameworks place the legal burden and accountability for accurate and timely disclosure squarely on the shoulders of the company's senior officers/board.

claim_a_snippet: Disclosures made under these regulations shall be disseminated to the stock exchanges where the securities are listed.
claim_b_snippet: The Form 8-K is filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission via EDGAR, making it immediately available to the public and exchanges.
labeler_note: Both systems ensure that once a disclosure is formalized, it is submitted directly to the central market authority/exchanges for immediate public consumption.

claim_a_snippet: Information may be withheld from public disclosure temporarily if it relates to a proposed transaction being explored under legitimate purposes with confidentiality agreements.
claim_b_snippet: Disclosure of a material definitive agreement or merger may be delayed until the agreement is fully executed, protecting ongoing confidential negotiations.
labeler_note: Both frameworks recognize that highly sensitive corporate negotiations (like mergers) can be kept confidential prior to reaching a definitive agreement.

claim_a_snippet: The board of directors shall ensure that a robust system of internal controls is in place to prevent the leakage of UPSI.
claim_b_snippet: Registrants must maintain effective disclosure controls and procedures to ensure that information required to be disclosed on Form 8-K is recorded, processed, and reported accurately.
labeler_note: Both regulations mandate that companies establish and maintain strict internal control procedures to identify and handle material information properly.

claim_a_snippet: Changes in Key Managerial Personnel (KMP) are deemed to be material events requiring careful handling.
claim_b_snippet: The departure, appointment, or election of directors and certain principal officers triggers a mandatory disclosure.
section_b: Item 5.02 - Departure and Appointment of Officers
labeler_note: Both regulators agree that shifts in top-tier executive leadership (C-suite/Directors) constitute material events that the market must know about.

claim_a_snippet: A company's failure to disclose material information promptly can result in severe regulatory penalties and sanctions.
claim_b_snippet: Failure to file a required Form 8-K can result in SEC enforcement actions, loss of Form S-3 eligibility, and civil penalties.
labeler_note: Both frameworks enforce strict regulatory penalties, including monetary fines and legal action, against companies that fail to make required material disclosures.

claim_a_snippet: Companies must ensure that all forward-looking information or earnings guidance is handled securely until officially published.
claim_b_snippet: Public announcements regarding results of operations or financial condition for a completed period must be formally furnished to the regulator.
section_a: Schedule A - Principles of Fair Disclosure
labeler_note: Both rules tightly control the release of financial results and operational guidance, ensuring they are distributed equitably to all investors simultaneously.

claim_a_snippet: Information relating to financial results, dividends, and capital structure are explicitly defined as UPSI. Mid-quarter impairments are not isolated as standalone mandatory disclosures outside of financial results.
claim_b_snippet: Item 2.06 requires a Form 8-K filing when a registrant's board of directors concludes that a material charge for impairment to one or more of its assets is required.
labeler_note: Reporting trigger mismatch. SEC 8-K requires an immediate, standalone filing specifically when a material impairment is concluded by the board. SEBI PIT treats general financial shifts as UPSI but lacks a standalone impairment trigger.

claim_a_snippet: UPSI includes any information that is likely to materially affect the price of the securities, focusing broadly on capital changes and mergers.
claim_b_snippet: Item 2.03 mandates a Form 8-K for the creation of a direct financial obligation or an obligation under an off-balance sheet arrangement of a registrant.
section_b: Item 2.03 - Creation of a Direct Financial Obligation
labeler_note: Specificity mismatch. SEC explicitly forces 8-K disclosure for the creation of significant debt or off-balance sheet arrangements. SEBI PIT does not explicitly tag routine debt creation as UPSI unless it alters the capital structure materially.

claim_a_snippet: UPSI generally does not encompass standard corporate governance document updates unless they fundamentally alter the business structure (like a merger).
claim_b_snippet: Item 5.03 requires an 8-K filing upon any amendment to the registrant's articles of incorporation or bylaws if the registrant has a class of equity securities registered.
section_a: Chapter I - Definition of UPSI - Bylaws
section_b: Item 5.03 - Amendments to Articles of Incorporation or Bylaws
labeler_note: Scope mismatch. SEC strictly requires a public 8-K filing for bylaw amendments. SEBI PIT does not classify generic bylaw amendments as price-sensitive information requiring insider trading blackout protocols.

claim_a_snippet: There are no provisions within the Insider Trading Regulations classifying a change in the financial/fiscal year as Unpublished Price Sensitive Information.
claim_b_snippet: Item 5.03 explicitly requires a Form 8-K to be filed if the registrant determines to change its fiscal year from that used in its most recent filing.
labeler_note: Scope mismatch. SEC requires a current report for changing the fiscal year. SEBI PIT ignores this completely as it is not inherently price-sensitive.

claim_a_snippet: Any amount collected by the company for violations of the code of conduct shall be remitted to the Board (SEBI) for credit to the Investor Protection and Education Fund. Waivers are not publicly broadcasted as price-sensitive.
claim_b_snippet: Item 5.05 requires a Form 8-K filing to publicly disclose any waiver, including an implicit waiver, from a provision of the code of ethics granted to the principal executive or financial officers.
section_b: Item 5.05 - Amendments to the Registrant's Code of Ethics
labeler_note: Transparency mismatch. SEBI requires companies to fine executives for code violations and report to SEBI. SEC 8-K requires companies to publicly announce to the market if they grant a waiver to a top executive regarding ethical codes.

claim_a_snippet: Routine voting results from general meetings are not classified as UPSI under PIT regulations, as they are public proceedings.
claim_b_snippet: Item 5.07 requires an 8-K filing within four business days to report the results of any matter that was submitted to a vote of security holders.
section_b: Item 5.07 - Submission of Matters to a Vote of Security Holders
labeler_note: Scope mismatch. SEC Form 8-K specifically captures and mandates the reporting of shareholder voting results. SEBI PIT does not govern the reporting of voting results.

claim_a_snippet: If UPSI is leaked or selectively disclosed, it must be made generally available promptly to avoid insider trading advantages.
claim_b_snippet: Under Regulation FD, if an unintentional selective disclosure of material nonpublic information occurs, the registrant must file an 8-K 'promptly', strictly defined as within 24 hours or the commencement of the next day's trading.
labeler_note: Numerical mismatch on cure periods. SEBI uses a qualitative 'promptly' for curing leaked UPSI. SEC defines 'promptly' for Reg FD cures with a hard 24-hour statutory deadline.

claim_a_snippet: Bankruptcy or receivership is governed under broader material events/UPSI, but does not have a dedicated, standalone clause in the PIT framework outlining receiver disclosures.
claim_b_snippet: Item 1.03 requires an 8-K filing specifically when a receiver, fiscal agent, or similar officer has been appointed for a registrant or its parent in a bankruptcy proceeding.
section_a: Chapter I - Definition of UPSI - Bankruptcy
labeler_note: Categorization mismatch. SEC has a dedicated 8-K item specifically for bankruptcy and receivership appointments. SEBI PIT groups this under general qualitative material events without standalone mechanics.

claim_a_snippet: Discovery of materially false financial statements is UPSI. The company handles disclosure generally under the obligation to promptly inform the stock exchange.
claim_b_snippet: Item 4.02 distinguishes between internal discovery of financial errors (Item 4.02(a)) and receiving formal notice from the independent auditor that past reports cannot be relied upon (Item 4.02(b)), requiring specific disclosures about the auditor's notice.
section_b: Item 4.02 - Non-Reliance on Previously Issued Financial Statements
labeler_note: Mechanism mismatch. SEC 8-K creates a bifurcated reporting requirement depending on whether management or the auditor discovered the financial error. SEBI PIT treats false financials universally as UPSI to be disclosed.

claim_a_snippet: Disclosures made under these regulations shall be made to the stock exchanges in such form as may be specified by them.
claim_b_snippet: Registrants must use the standardized SEC Form 8-K and file it electronically through the SEC's Electronic Data Gathering, Analysis, and Retrieval (EDGAR) system.
labeler_note: Filing mechanism mismatch. SEBI allows disclosures in whatever form the specific stock exchange dictates. SEC mandates a singular federal form (8-K) filed through a specific federal database (EDGAR).
